Title: Dedication and commitment was our key driver during the COVID-19 pandemic
NewsSummary: Dr Nancy Kunyiha shares her experience on how the department coped with the challenges posed by COVID-19 pandemic
NewsContent:
​Dr Nancy Kunyiha has been with Aga Khan University since 2004. She is currently the interim chair, department of Internal Medicine. As we celebrate International Women’s Day, she shares her experience on how the department coped with the challenges posed by COVID-19 pandemic.

How did the COVID-19 pandemic disrupt your work and plans for 2020?

The COVID-19 pandemic was a time of immense change and transition for me as I took on a new leadership role as the interim chair of the department of internal medicine in May 2020. Leading the largest department at the Medical College in East Africa at the onset of the greatest pandemic in our lifetime was challenging. Decisions had to be made, regular care and teaching had to go on. Some of my colleagues were infected and needed support. I had conferences to attend and travel plans to take my son to university.

How did you manage to get things going during this time?

Teamwork held us together in good stead. I realized from the beginning that a pandemic could not be managed by a single individual however accomplished they were. My role was to define the urgent tasks, identify the most appropriate individuals to undertake those tasks and equip and trust them to deliver on the tasks assigned. 

As a department, we have a dedicated and committed team of residents, fellows, faculty and active medical staff in medicine and my role was to engage, co-ordinate, encourage and motivate them to put their best foot forward in extremely difficult and stressful times. I had excellent support team from the administration and a superb programme director. In addition, as the head of the Kenya Diabetes Study group I championed the writing of a statement for persons with diabetes at the beginning of the COVID-19 pandemic. 

What was the impact of your input? 

By mobilizing specialists in a rapidly changing context. The team created the COVID-19 protocols that we were able to ensure up-to-date decisions on patient care, for example Thromboprophylaxis (prevention of clots inside the blood vessels) in COVID-19. In addition, care of COVID-19 in the field hospital and protocols on which patients were to be admitted there and the level of their care. Treatment protocols for COVID-19 that have been evolving over the year. 

We achieved treatment and recovery rates that were well within international standards. In addition, we are able to change clinic flows and structure, use telemedicine to reduce wait times, ease congestion to ensure patient safety while accessing care. 

How long did it take you to manage the disruption? 

There was an acute disruption that took a few weeks to adapt but the chronic disruption continues as the COVID-19 pandemic continues to unfold. We have learnt to live and engage with the challenges as they come along.

Any key memorable moments or incidents that happened during this time?

The devastation of losing the first young COVID-19 patient early during the pandemic but also months down the line, being thanked by a patient who made it through critical COVID-19 condition with tears in his eyes for the nights he was isolated and alone in the ICU section.

What were the key lessons from this?

Human beings have an inherent capacity to survive the unknown even in the face of our own mortality, adapt, and thrive. The power of teamwork cannot be overestimated and that we need each other to be successful in any endeavours.

How did you manage to balance family life and work amidst the COVID-19 pandemic? 

My family kept me balanced. I tried to ensure that I sat down to have dinner with my family in the evenings. The weekends were quieter with less movement so we spent more time together reading, playing games, sometimes just sitting at the fireplace quietly together. My young adult children took on some of my domestic roles. I have tried to safely keep in touch with family and friends.

What do you think about AKU and women empowerment? 

AKU has been at the forefront of empowering women with many of us being promoted to leadership roles within the organisation. This has been very encouraging to us and makes us motivated to achieve more within the workplace.

Anything else you feel we can do to meet the goal of an equal future?

Consider flexi working hours for female health care practitioners.

What is your message for IWD 2021 to your fellow AKU colleagues?

Women in the Kenyan work place are largely less assertive and often bypassed for leadership roles. However, the women in leadership across the world have demonstrated the power of engagement, foresight and planning during COVID-19 pandemic. Women have shown that power is not only physical but that the power of resilience, compassion and empathy with good decision-making can transform the working environments and communities that we serve. I am honored to be in leadership at this time in history and bring my uniqueness to the all the spaces I am in – family, clinical, teaching, board room and mentoring, with the hope that I will leave transformative engagements and be the light to those around me and the next generation.
